reason: Direct Wisconsin State Climatology Office, Peshtigo Fire Museum, and National Weather Service hosted receipts support all seven spoken beats; a fresh render and human review remain required.
story: On October 8–9, 1871, dry conditions and strong southwest winds fanned smoldering fires in northeastern Wisconsin. A firestorm consumed Peshtigo in less than two hours. Father Peter Pernin survived after taking refuge in the river, as described in his own account quoted by the local fire museum. Only two buildings remained. The Wisconsin State Climatology Office estimates 1,200–2,500 deaths and calls it the deadliest wildfire in U.S. history. The Great Chicago Fire burned on the same night and received far more lasting attention.
angle: The deadliest wildfire in U.S. history consumed Peshtigo in less than two hours while Chicago burned that same night.

claims.claim: The Wisconsin State Climatology Office estimates 1,200–2,500 deaths in the Peshtigo Fire.
The Peshtigo Fire occurred October 8–9, 1871, after a warm, dry period that reduced moisture in dead logs, branches, and brush.
A pressure difference generated strong southwest winds that fanned smoldering fires across Wisconsin and Michigan by evening.
A firestorm formed, and Peshtigo was consumed in less than two hours.
Father Peter Pernin survived after taking refuge in the river; his eyewitness account describes being in the river for a long time.
Only two buildings remained standing in Peshtigo after the fire.
The Wisconsin State Climatology Office calls the Peshtigo Fire the deadliest wildfire in U.S. history.
The Great Chicago Fire burned the same night; a contemporary retrospective hosted by NWS says Chicago continued to attract headlines while Peshtigo received little notice outside the region.

disputed: Neither the Wisconsin State Climatology Office nor the checked local sources establish the old spoken 110 mph wind or 2,000°F temperature. Both figures and their visual cards were removed.
The old narration said the river was freezing and Chicago was 400 miles south; these precise descriptions are not needed and have been removed.
The death toll is an estimate ranging from 1,200 to 2,500, not an exact count; the hook says “up to.”

The National Weather Service page republishes a Green Bay Press-Gazette retrospective with permission. Its Chicago-headlines observation is attributed to that retrospective, not independent NWS meteorological research.
